item.title: Anti-Environmentalism and the Future of Green Growth
item.content:encoded:
Anastasios Xepapadeas, Athens University of Economics and Business

Simone Marsiglio, University of Pisa

Luca Gori, University of Pisa

In recent years, the global transition toward sustainable and low-carbon economic systems has encountered increasing political and social resistance. This phenomenon—broadly termed "anti-environmentalism"—encompasses a range of behaviors, beliefs, and policy stances that oppose or undermine environmental regulation, renewable energy expansion, and climate mitigation efforts. While green growth remains a central framework for reconciling economic development with ecological preservation, its implementation is increasingly conditioned by public acceptance, political will, and institutional credibility. Understanding how and why opposition to environmental policy arises—and how it interacts with economic incentives and policy design—is therefore a critical problem from both policy and academic perspectives.

It is therefore essential to examine the implications for pathways toward green growth and sustainable development when environmental considerations—particularly those related to climate change—are neglected under the influence of anti-environmentalist attitudes. This concern is made more urgent by scientific evidence indicating that climate change increases both the frequency and magnitude of extreme events, thereby amplifying expected damages. Moreover, the growing likelihood of transgressing critical planetary boundaries underscores the importance of understanding anti-environmentalist movements, which, if embedded in policy, could accelerate such boundary crossings. In addition, anti-environmentalist positions may hinder the mechanisms of creative destruction that facilitate transitions to low-carbon economies, offering a further area of relevance for the proposed Special Issue.

This Special Issue will bring together leading research in environmental economics, macroeconomics, political economy, and behavioral economics to explore the drivers, dynamics, and implications of anti-environmentalism for sustainable growth. It aims to provide a comprehensive analysis of how economic systems can maintain progress toward green growth amidst political polarization and societal backlash. We welcome a broad range of techniques and approaches, including optimal control, game theory, political economy, and network theory. Special attention will be given to methodological (theoretical, empirical or experimental) contributions aiming at disentangling the multifaceted nature of the anti-environmentalism and green growth relationship.

This Call for Papers is related to the HEDGE (Health, Environment, Development and Growth Economics) conference which will take place in Pisa on 5-7 February 2026, but it is open to everyone. Both conference participants and non-participants are encouraged to submit high-quality papers dealing with topics related to anti-environmentalism and green growth, broadly defined.

Potential topics

  • Economic, social and political determinants of anti-environmental attitudes and behavior
  • The impact of populism, misinformation, and lobbying on climate and environmental policy outcomes
  • Public perception and resistance to carbon taxation, green industrial policies, and regulation
  • Distributional and equity aspects of green growth as sources of policy backlash
  • The role of institutions and governance in shaping environmental resistance
  • International and comparative analyses of anti-environmental movements and climate cooperation
  • Behavioral and cultural dimensions of environmental skepticism and pro-growth narratives
  • Policy strategies for overcoming anti-environmentalist sentiment and fostering green, just and inclusive transitions
  • Economic growth under increasing climate-related extreme event risk, and the costs of climate skepticism

Timeline

  • March 31, 2027: Submission deadline

item.title: Wildfires in a Changing Climate: Impacts, Adaptation, and Policy
item.content:encoded:
Sarah Meier, ETH Zurich

Eric Strobl, University of Bern

Robert J. R. Elliott, University of Birmingham

In many regions of the world fire seasons have been lengthening, alongside increases in wildfire frequency and intensity. Climate change, shifts in land use, and the expansion of human settlements into fire-prone areas have transformed wildfires from largely localised hazards into systemic risks with cascading effects across ecosystems and economies. These developments have rendered many existing models, policies, and assumptions increasingly outdated, underscoring the urgent need for robust economic evidence to inform policy and private-sector decision making aligned with current and future wildfire conditions.

Wildfires and smoke pollution affect economies through multiple, interconnected channels. Beyond direct suppression costs and physical damages, wildfires disrupt production and supply chains, reduce labour productivity, influence tourism and recreation, and reshape migration and housing-market dynamics. Smoke exposure generates substantial public health burdens and impairs cognitive performance and labour market outcomes. These impacts occur within a context of rising public expenditures on prevention, suppression, and recovery, as well as rapidly evolving policy debates around insurance markets, land-use regulation, adaptation, and risk financing. Together, these dynamics highlight the need for empirical research that quantifies welfare consequences and evaluates the effectiveness of emerging policy responses.

Despite growing attention, many ecological and economic impacts of wildfires and smoke, particularly with regard to their persistence, remain under-studied, especially in regions that have not historically experienced large-scale wildfires but are now facing emerging risks. Cross-regional comparison can therefore support knowledge exchange between regions with long-standing fire experience and those facing emerging vulnerabilities, including across the Global North and South. At the same time, recent advances in data availability, remote sensing, and the use of AI-based technologies for monitoring, early warning, and suppression create new opportunities for applied research.

This Special Issue seeks contributions that advance empirical and policy-relevant understanding of wildfire impacts, as well as analyses that evaluate adaptation and management strategies aimed at reducing their welfare costs. We welcome applied research grounded in environmental, climate, and resource economics, including studies that use new data or innovative identification strategies to address this emerging challenge. Interdisciplinary work is encouraged where it strengthens economic insight into wildfire impacts and informs policy decisions.

Potential topics

  • Labour productivity, sectoral employment shifts, and worker mobility
  • Housing markets, mortgage risk, and migration and other behavioural responses to wildfire risk and exposure
  • Natural capital and ecosystem service valuation, including impacts on biodiversity, recreation, and forest asset pricing
  • Inequality, information access, and distributional impacts of exposure and monitoring technologies
  • Public finance, insurance markets, and the fiscal consequences for local and regional governments
  • Institutions, governance, and risk-sharing arrangements, including coordination across jurisdictions, public-private roles, and firm responses to wildfire risk
  • Prevention, suppression, and adaptation strategies, including land-use planning, prescribed burning, indigenous fire stewardship, and advanced monitoring and management technologies
  • Welfare losses from smoke exposure, including physical and mental health outcomes and associated human capital effects

Timeline

  • September 30, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Valuing health and longevity: Advances and innovations
item.content:encoded:
Lisa A. Robinson, Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health

Olof Bystrom, OECD

Ståle Navrud, Norwegian University of Life Sciences

Mortality risk reductions typically dominate the benefits estimates for environmental policies. Recent reviews and syntheses of the value per statistical life (VSL) literature suggest that, while the research base is relatively strong for some settings, it contains significant gaps and inconsistencies. These include the need for more research on how attributes of the population and the risk affect these values. Deciding how to best synthesize and apply the estimates is also challenging.

The value of nonfatal risk reductions receives substantially less attention, although the expected reduction in cases of nonfatal illnesses or injuries associated with environmental policies is frequently large. As is the case for mortality risks, estimates of individual willingness to pay (WTP) are the preferred measure of values. However, due to gaps in the research literature, these risks are often valued using proxies such as averted costs.

Current approaches to valuation also raise a number of questions such as how to appropriately combine values for co-occurring effects and how to address distributional equity. Recent and emerging research addresses all of these problems, including new best practice WTP studies for mortality and morbidity, improved approaches for combining results across studies and transferring the estimates to different contexts, and innovations to address related challenges.

This special issue will highlight important contributions to this work and provide a useful reference for those interested in applying or building upon the results.

Potential topics

  • Value per statistical life (VSL) and population attributes affecting mortality risk valuations
  • Valuation of nonfatal risk reductions and morbidity using willingness to pay approaches
  • Synthesis and application of health valuation estimates across different contexts
  • Addressing co-occurring effects and distributional equity in health valuations
  • Benefit transfer methods and meta-analysis approaches for health valuation
  • Best practice willingness to pay studies for mortality and morbidity risk reductions
  • Combining and transferring valuation estimates to different policy contexts
  • Methodological innovations in environmental health economic evaluation

Timeline

  • October 31, 2026: Submission deadline

item.title: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP): trends and reflections
item.content:encoded:
Sanchayan Banerjee, King's College London

Lory Barile, University of Warwick

Traditional environmental economics addresses market failures (e.g., externalities, public goods, asymmetric information), using regulation and price-based instruments under a rational choice benchmark. Decades of evidence on bounded rationality, bounded self-interest, and bounded willpower reveal systematic departures from that benchmark, generating behavioural failures that can blunt or distort policy. These departures are well documented across core domains (e.g., environmental valuation, discounting of future outcomes and assets, and utility maximisation) and have given rise to a vibrant subfield: Behavioural Environmental Economics & Policy (BEEP).

This Special Issue will consolidate and showcase new contributions and evidence on how behavioural insights improve the design, delivery, and evaluation of environmental policy. Although BEEP has grown substantially, few efforts have mapped its diverse applications. We aim to fill this gap by providing theoretical, actionable, and evidence-based guidance for researchers and practitioners on putting BEEP into practice. Framed this way, the Special Issue will serve as a practical reference, grounded in recent cases that show why recognising and addressing human behaviour (and its failures) is essential to tackling urgent challenges, from climate change and biodiversity loss to air and water pollution.

We welcome conceptual/theoretical, empirical, and policy-oriented submissions that apply behavioural insights to understand, explain, or solve environmental problems. We particularly encourage quantitative, qualitative, and mixed-method designs (e.g., field/lab experiments, quasi-/natural experiments, RCTs, process evaluations), though literature reviews and theoretical contributions will also be considered. Overall, we seek contributions that diagnose and integrate market and behavioural failures and that design, test, and evaluate policies, including 'green nudges', that are both effective and welfare-enhancing.

Potential topics

  • Interactions between market failures and behavioural failures in environmental settings
  • Policy design that combines prices/standards with behavioural tools (defaults, salience/framing, simplification, commitment)
  • Welfare analysis (including psychological costs), ethics, and paternalism in environmental policy
  • Empirical identification of behavioural mechanisms; field/lab/quasi-experimental evidence
  • Heterogeneity, equity, and distributional consequences of behavioural environmental policies
  • Replication, meta-analysis, and open-science practices in this domain
  • Choice architecture and environmental outcomes
  • Interactions between behavioural instruments and prices/regulation
  • Welfare measurement and persistence (including psychological costs)
  • Distributional and equity dimensions
  • Climate cognition and communication
  • Evaluation and methods

Timeline

  • November 30, 2026: Submission deadline
